idiom_name: hand-written or macro-generated forwarding impl (ambassador / dynamic-proxy)
implementation_notes: Rust has no reflection and cannot define a type at run time, so the forwarding type is produced at compile time: either written by hand or expanded from an attribute macro (ambassador's #[delegatable_trait] plus #[derive(Delegate)], or the dynamic-proxy crate, which turns a trait into calls on a single interceptor carrying an InvocationInfo payload of argument names, values and return type). Deref-based wrappers cover the case where no member needs intercepting, and a wrapper can be stored behind dyn Trait when the implementation must stay interchangeable. Unknown members are a compile error, so the dynamic part of the pattern is deliberately traded away for static dispatch and type safety.
pitfalls: Deref coercion silently redirects method calls to the inner type when the wrapper does not define them, so a forgotten override is invisible in review and only shows up as missing instrumentation.
Macro-generated delegation cannot forward associated types and constants automatically and breaks on generic where-clauses, producing compile errors inside expanded code.
The wrapper is a distinct type: trait-object identity, Any downcasts and type-level APIs see LoggingService<X>, never X.
There is no interception of members the trait does not declare - adding one to the call side is a compile error rather than a dynamic lookup failure.
